Question six. What is the difference between additive, semi-additive, and non-additive measures? Revenue is additive: it sums across every dimension. A balance is semi-additive. Across accounts on one day, it sums fine: sixteen hundred dollars at the end of March. Across time, it doesn't: the quarter's three month-ends add up to forty-eight hundred, money nobody ever had. Over time, take the closing balance, or the average. Non-additive measures, like ratios and distinct counts, sum across nothing. Three users on Monday and three on Tuesday were four people. Recount them from the rows at the grain.

Question seven. Why should you avoid storing percentages or ratios directly in fact tables? Because every roll-up gets them wrong. Take two orders, with margins of fifty and ten percent. Sum them, and the margin is sixty percent. Average them, and it's thirty. The real margin is fourteen, because the ten percent order carries nine-tenths of the revenue. So store the additive parts, gross revenue and cost of goods sold, and divide after summing. A ratio of sums weighs each order by its revenue. A stored percentage has forgotten that weight.

Question eight. What is a role-playing dimension? One physical table used several times by one fact, in different roles. Each order here has three date keys: ordered, shipped and delivered. So the date dimension is joined three times, under three aliases. Order one oh one was placed on March first, shipped on the third, and delivered on the seventh. Kept once, it answers what no single role can: order to delivery took six point seven days on average, nine at most. For BI tools, give each role its own view, with columns named for it, like ship date, so nobody filters on the wrong date.
